title: Deliberate Practice: A Universal Learning Method — Online Reader Framework
buttons: Techniques for Deciding What to Practice
content:
About This Guide
What is this about?

Standard advice on learning often fails the people who need it most. We are frequently told that to practice we must spend many hours repeating the same thing many times and that this will eventually lead to mastery, but rarely are we told how to spend those hours. Many dedicated learners simply repeat the same mistakes for years rather than correcting them. They hit plateaus and eventually give up, assuming they simply lack the necessary talent. This guide addresses that specific gap.

Most existing literature on "Deliberate Practice" focuses on elite performers—chess grandmasters, Olympic athletes, or concert violinists—who have access to world-class coaches and established training programs. That advice is useless if you are trying to improve your academic writing alone in a library or learning a foreign language without a tutor. I wanted to translate the principles of high-performance psychology into a practical toolkit for anybody.

title: Building Your Language Muscle — Online Reader Framework
content:
What is this

This is a guide for you, the language student. It is aimed at students of any language but it contains an appendix focusing on how to apply this to learning Czech. It is about a new way of learning called deliberate practice. It will tell you how you can succeed if you work hard and smart. Here’s the key advice:

Think about your teacher as your coach and your class as a place to get feedback. All the hard work will happen outside of class.
Set very specific goals for your learning. Not just to learn a language but also what you actually want to be able to say after a set amount time.
Think about the aim of learning as overcoming the limits of working memory by building up bigger and richer chunks of language.
Organise your learning into 6-week sprints and plan to spend at least 20 hours in each sprint on focused practice.
Practice in smaller, more frequent segments, but have at least some 30 minute or longer intensive practice sessions.

content:
What's the difference between phonetics and phonology?

I'm surprised that nobody has mentioned the form/function distinction.

Phonetics studies the nature (acoustic and articulatory) of sounds that humans produce while speaking. Phonology studies their function in differentiating meaning in various contexts.

Thus (very crudely), phonetics will notice the difference between the aspirated and non-aspirated /p/ in pin vs. spin. But phonology will be mostly interested in the fact that the meaning of both words will change when you replace /p/ with /k/, in exactly the same way as in lip vs. lick where aspiration doesn't enter the picture.

But of course, phonology can only be successful when it has good phonetics to rely on.
